column3: It repeats the command before the same irreversible day and adds the ensuing separation of people.
The recurring rejection of messengers gives a broad backdrop for the command to respond, but adds little about the final day.
Its catalogue of sought refuges sharply contrasts with the focus's declaration that no refuge will remain.
It specifies worldly means unavailable on that day, extending the focus's announcement of no recourse.
The immediately preceding verse denies protectors and any path once God leads astray, directly framing the focus's no-refuge warning.
It shows people delaying faith and forgiveness until punishment confronts them, clarifying the urgency to respond beforehand.
It establishes the day as one in which no person can avail another and authority belongs wholly to God.
Its contrast of transient worldly enjoyment with what endures with God supplies only a broad motive for timely response.
It presents turning to God as the only refuge, a deliberate counterpart to the final absence of any refuge.
Wrongdoers ask for delay under punishment so they can answer the call, directly exposing the belated response the focus prevents.
The terse statement about persistent transgression does not clarify response, the day, refuge, or denial.
It portrays an actual response to God and the Messenger after hardship, a positive but situational counterpart to the focus's summons.
God's exclusive dominion and the absence of any guardian or helper support the focus's loss of recourse.
It immediately depicts wrongdoers, after seeing punishment, asking for a route back when no route remains.
Abraham's unease at visitors who do not eat does not illuminate the final summons or closed refuge.
Its call to recognize revelation when challengers cannot respond supplies a limited parallel to answering the divine call.
Patience and forgiveness in the preceding discourse offer an ethical response, but do not clarify the irreversible day.
Human attempts to turn believers back from faith are a different kind of return from the focus's finality.
It explicitly says that what God wills cannot be repelled and that no protector remains besides Him.
The command to the Prophet not to obey opponents is a distant form of obedience, not the final response addressed here.
It identifies denial and arrogance as the inner posture of those rejecting the Hereafter, illuminating the focus's loss of denial.
It directly commands believers to answer God and the Messenger, and joins that response to life and eventual gathering to Him.
It shows that disputation after the response has arrived collapses into wrath and severe punishment.
God's answer to a plea for help provides a positive, earlier-time counterpart to the focus's closed final situation.
It states that faith or later goodness will not benefit when decisive signs arrive, directly defining the expired opportunity.
The destruction of better-appointed former generations does not add a distinct element to the focus's warning.
Its historical pattern of rejecting messengers only broadly reinforces the warning and is redundant with earlier rejection examples.
The summons to worship, seek forgiveness, and turn back to the near responsive Lord gives the available pre-final alternative.
God responding to believers who do good gives a positive counterpart to the imperative, though without the final-day boundary.
Its regulated return in a marital ruling is only contrast evidence and does not illuminate final return or refuge.
The reminder that earlier deniers were rejected adds a general warning already supplied more specifically above.
It commands turning and surrendering before punishment arrives, after which no help will be given.
Calling unfamiliar visitors an unknown people does not bear on the focus's denial or final day.
The limitation of intercession on that day qualifies the focus's announcement that no recourse remains.
God's acceptance of repentance and pardon clarifies the presently open alternative before the threatened closure.
It joins return to God with the Fire for transgressors, adding a judgment destination to the focus's irreversible day.
Calling that day difficult reinforces its severity but adds no account of response or lost refuge.
It commands following revelation before sudden punishment arrives, closely paralleling the focus's time-bounded imperative.
The deniers' question about being returned to a former state supplies only a limited contrast to irreversibility.
After fulfillment, people seek intercessors or a return to act differently, directly portraying an impossible late remedy.
God as sole protector and raiser of the dead offers a broad theological ground, not the focus's closed final condition.
The opening notice of Pharaoh's people's trial does not clarify the summons or the irreversible day.
The punishment of deniers is a generic warning and adds little after the more direct finality passages.
The statement that the Book descends from God does not by itself clarify the required response or its deadline.
Being turned back from faith by others concerns a different kind of return from the final non-return in the focus.
God's awareness of people on that day supplies a general judgment setting but no further account of refuge or response.
The continuity of revelation across messengers gives only a remote context for answering the Lord.
Following disbelievers and turning back in loss is a different, worldly reversal from the focus's irreversible outcome.
The destruction of past rejecting peoples repeats a general warning without a distinct connection to response or refuge.
The description of invoking false deities does not materially explain the final summons.
Joseph's foreknowledge of provisions and rejection of an unbelieving creed do not clarify the focus's final boundary.
It warns that people await angels or their Lord's command and stresses that their wrongdoing is their own.
It depicts those who answer their Lord through worship, consultation, and giving, the positive lived counterpart to the focus's command.
The question about denying God's signs identifies the denial that the focus says will no longer be possible.
Its doctrinal correction and call to faith do not add a specific account of the final day or recourse.
Noah's grateful servitude is not connected to the focus's warning.
Its demand for authority behind claims of divinity offers only a broad response-to-signs context.
Demanding punishment rather than answering rebuke gives a limited contrary posture, but not the final closure itself.
The conclusion that all affairs journey to God supplies the destination for the day announced in the focus.
The greeting between Abraham and unfamiliar visitors does not clarify the focus.
It presents punishment followed by return to the Lord for a greater punishment, adding a judgment sequence.
Its individual responsibility and prior sending of a messenger provide an accountability frame for the call to respond.
The brief identification of Noah's people as transgressors adds no distinct element.
It pictures people turning away on the day with no protector from God, closely paralleling the focus's absence of refuge.
God's power to gather creation provides a broad eschatological premise but not the focus's summons or finality.
Recognizing God's favor and then denying it illuminates the denial posture that will be unavailable on that day.
It similarly urges present obedience before a day with no exchange or friendship, though that warning is now partly redundant.
Its command to establish the religion and not divide gives a nearby content for the Lord's call, without the deadline.
Being forgotten on the day after forgetting God's signs gives a reciprocal consequence for refusing the present communication.
It removes kin and children as sources of benefit on the Day of Resurrection, extending the focus's no-refuge horizon.
Its contrast of truth with misguidance and turning away is too general to define the final loss of response.
The demand to hasten one's portion before the Day of Account shows defiant haste, but not the focus's core warning.
At death a person asks for a short delay to act righteously, vividly clarifying an unextendable deadline for response.
Revelation as light that guides to a straight path supplies the means by which the focus's command can be answered.
Once the Lord's command has come, punishment is not repelled, marking the same transition from open appeal to final execution.
Timed praise before sunrise and sunset does not materially clarify the final day despite its temporal language.
The affirmation that the Prophet is a messenger only indirectly supports the call addressed through him.
Moses' objection to the killing of a youth does not illuminate response, refuge, or the final day.
The security of the righteous from the greatest terror gives a general contrast but no account of the focus's injunction.
The nearby command to call, stand upright, and affirm accountability before God gives a practical response trajectory.
Repeated turning away when signs come describes the refusal that makes the focus's warning necessary.
God alone gives life and death, and no guardian or helper exists besides Him, directly supporting the no-refuge declaration.
The modes of divine speech give context for receiving revelation but not the final consequence of refusing it.
Joseph recognizing his brothers while they do not recognize him does not clarify final denial or refuge.
The imminent day leaves wrongdoers without an intimate ally or an obeyed intercessor, directly expanding the focus's no recourse.
The immediate continuation treats turning away from the messenger and limits his duty to delivering the message.
The grant of scripture for guidance is only a general antecedent to the call to respond.
The question on why they do not help one another supplies a compact judgment-scene parallel to the lack of aid.
Demanding angels as proof risks bringing the decisive event that closes the testing period, a cautionary contrast to timely response.
The challenge to idols for failing to speak is not a final-day account of denial or refuge.
Its woe for deniers on that day reinforces the judgment consequence, though without the focus's specific closure.
Return to God as true master for rapid judgment supplies the destination and authority behind the focus's warning.
It offers repentance before painful punishment and again denies any guardian or helper, though in a broader setting.
The fate of earlier polytheists offers a historical warning but is redundant after the closer passages on refusal.
The command to invite to the Lord's way with wise exhortation identifies the present means of answering the summons.
Past and possible future betrayal do not clarify the final day, refuge, or response.
Its instruction to verify claims in travel concerns social judgment, not the focus's irreversible divine judgment.
The certainty that the Hour will come supplies the event whose arrival the focus says cannot be turned back.
Faith guiding the heart amid calamity offers a broad theological response but no final-day closure.
Prior disbelief producing a now-distant, inaccessible position illustrates the accumulated irreversibility warned of in the focus.
It warns of a day when no soul can answer for another and neither intercession nor ransom is accepted.
It repeats the individual liability and unavailable intercession or aid of the final day.
It distinguishes timely repentance from the invalid repentance claimed only when death has arrived.
It names Hell as the wrongdoers' refuge and denies that they will find any escape from it.
Before the Fire, deniers wish they could return and no longer deny God's signs, a direct late reversal wish.
It denies that any ransom or intercession can rescue a soul after it is held to account.
At the sight of punishment, every wrongdoer would offer all earthly wealth as ransom and conceals regret.
Once wrongdoers see punishment, it is neither lightened for them nor delayed.
The guilty see the Fire, know they will fall into it, and find no way to turn away from it.
It describes the time when disbelievers cannot ward the Fire from their faces or backs and receive no help.
Whenever they seek to leave the Fire in anguish, they are returned to it.
At death, the wrongdoer asks, "My Lord, send me back," directly exposing the belated appeal.
It refuses that requested return and places a barrier until the day people are raised.
Criminals ask to be returned so that they may act righteously after seeing and hearing the truth.
Forgetting the meeting of this day is answered by being forgotten and tasting the lasting punishment.
It depicts wrongdoers before their Lord after the promise has come true, blaming one another too late.
The people of the Fire call for release to act righteously, and are answered that their warning period was sufficient.
The soul's regret for neglecting its duty to God gives voice to the missed opportunity before final judgment.
It records the later claim that guidance would have made the speaker among the God-conscious.
Seeing punishment, the speaker wishes for another return in order to do good.
It recalls that people were called to faith but disbelieved, directly identifying the earlier refused summons.
The people of the Fire acknowledge death and life and ask for a way out, an especially close counterpart to no refuge and no denial.
The Fire's inhabitants dispute responsibility after punishment, showing the futility of post-judgment argument.
Those followed deny that they can avert any portion of the Fire from their followers.
It shows the wrongdoers exposed to the Fire and defines true loss as loss on the Day of Resurrection.
The guilty remain in the punishment of Hell without relief.
A barrier closes off hypocrites seeking the believers' light, a vivid image of irreversible exclusion.
Disbelievers are told not to make excuses that day, directly paralleling the loss of any denial or revision.
No intimate friend will ask after an intimate friend on the day of judgment, extending the focus's absence of refuge.
The guilty person would ransom himself with children, spouse, brother, and all on earth, yet cannot escape.
It commands fear of the day of return to God, when every soul is fully repaid for what it earned.
On the day each soul finds its deeds present, the evildoer wishes a vast distance between itself and its evil.
Neither earth's fill of gold nor any ransom is accepted from those who disbelieve and die in that state.
Even all that is on earth twice over cannot ransom the disbelievers from the punishment of the day.
Being set before their Lord makes the denied reality undeniable, directly anticipating the focus's loss of denial.
The gathering day compresses worldly life to a brief encounter and exposes mutual recognition among those who denied meeting God.
It names the day when humanity will be gathered and witnessed, strengthening the focus's announced day.
All appear before God, and followers learn that those they relied on cannot avert any part of God's punishment.
It warns not to think God unaware of wrongdoers, but delaying them to the day when eyes will stare.
On the transformed earth and heavens, people emerge before the One, the Overpowering.
Every person's record is fastened to them and will be produced open on the Day of Resurrection.
It commands warning of the Day of Regret, when the matter is decided while people had remained heedless.
All faces are humbled before the Ever-Living Sustainer, and the bearer of wrongdoing fails.
When the trumpet is blown, kinship ties and mutual inquiry no longer operate among people.
Cast bound into a narrow place in the Fire, its people call out for destruction.
On the Hour's arrival, the guilty fall into despair.
The disbelievers in the Fire are neither allowed to die nor is its punishment lightened for them.
On that day no soul is wronged at all; each is repaid only for what it did.
The command to separate from the criminals on that day makes final division explicit.
It identifies Hell as the one promised to persistent deniers.
The disbelievers are driven to Hell in groups after its gates are opened and their warnings recalled.
On the day people emerge, nothing about them is hidden from God and all dominion is His alone.
Whether they endure or plead, the Fire remains their lodging and no appeal is accepted.
It warns wrongdoers of the punishment of a painful day after their dispute divided them.
God's dominion over heaven and earth culminates in the day the Hour rises, when falsifiers lose.
No angelic intercession avails except after God's permission, reinforcing the lack of independent recourse.
The human being asks on that day where there is any escape.
It answers that there is no refuge.
It fixes the destination on that day as return to the Lord.
Receiving one's record from behind one's back depicts the condemned side of final accounting.
